slides.title: SRAM levers are not comparable by size — they are ranked by when the price is paid
slides.caption: A merit order of the KV-capacity levers: x is resident KV tokens, each block is a lever in price order, colour is when the cost is paid (P0 boot, P1 per turn, P2 per decode step, P3 accuracy), hatching means not device-verified, and the red line is the 167K score-buffer wall. Produced from machine-readable price cards written for the SRAM-performance exchange methodology. It settled that there is no single formula: prices in different currencies are comparable only under a stated workload profile. Analytical, built on compiled constants.
slides.notes: Round 5. Sources: analyses/2026-09-02-sram-perf-exchange/ (levers.json) and docs/design/2026-09-02-sram-performance-exchange-methodology.md. No device job. Caveats the report attaches: unpriced levers stay hatched and are never assumed free; capacities are re-derived after every composition change; the per-step price of the near pool (95K) and far pool (167K) has never been measured. The 167K wall itself is the per-slot 32 B of softmax scratch that cannot be parked (Round 4).

slides.title: The first demand curve was wrong: calling an over-capacity session infeasible collapsed the shared-pool line
slides.caption: Version 1 of G(C), the prefill tokens avoided per call as a function of resident KV capacity C, replayed on 1,048 local Claude Code contexts. Its shared-pool line collapses below 256K, which is an artifact of declaring any session larger than C infeasible rather than a property of the workload. Kept for the record only; F3 is the corrected curve. Measured trace replay with an analytical residency model.
slides.notes: Round 7; Le's correction. File lives in agent-memory (assets/2026-09-02-gc-demand-curve.png), not the repo. Two reasons not to quote numbers off it: the infeasibility rule, and the fact that the underlying trace was later found to contain 58,581 duplicate rows (Round 28). F3 is both re-ruled and regenerated.

slides.title: How much prefill a resident-KV capacity actually avoids, and what the next rung is worth
slides.caption: Version 2 replaces the infeasibility rule with best-effort prefix residency: an LRU trims tails and any missing prefix is recomputed, which lands the shared-pool line within 15-20% of the single-request curve. The marginal value of capacity is dG/dC = P(context > C) — 0.93 at 32K, 0.80 at 64K, 0.51 at 167K. Measured trace replay of 46,650 de-duplicated API calls.
slides.notes: Round 7, regenerated after the Round 28 de-duplication. Script and data in analyses/2026-09-02-gc-trace-study/. Caveats: Claude tokenizer, one power user, one harness, one month; and per Round 35 these are frontier-model context depths (median 302K per call), so read the deep rungs as an upper bound on what a 4B deployment would need.

slides.title: The provider keeps KV about an hour, and intra-turn gaps are 10.9 s — keeping across a turn is unconditionally right
slides.caption: Idle-gap distributions inside a turn and at turn starts, next to the share of context the provider re-created as a function of gap length. It re-created 3.7% of context for gaps under five minutes and 95.9% beyond an hour. Measured directly from the usage fields of 46,650 de-duplicated Claude Code API calls.
slides.notes: Round 7, regenerated after Round 28 (the intra-turn gap p50 moved from 3.3 s to 10.9 s when duplicate streamed records were removed — which makes keeping more clearly right, not less). analyses/2026-09-02-gc-trace-study/. What it cannot price: turn-boundary contention, which needs a multi-tenant trace this study does not have.

slides.title: Recompute is never the right recovery above ~25K tokens; without a host mirror, eviction is the most expensive option
slides.caption: Break-even idle gap for the three recoveries — keep, reload, recompute — against context length. With a host mirror at the 12.5 GB/s design rate, reloading any context up to 256K takes less than the median intra-turn gap; without one, the measured 1.37-1.44 GB/s egress makes eviction the worst option. Decode tok/s cancels in keep-versus-reload: it sets the stakes, not the crossover. Measured gaps and measured link rates, modelled economics.
slides.notes: Round 7. Link rates: host-to-wafer 3.2 GB/s and wafer-to-host 1.37-1.44 GB/s are measured; 12.5 GB/s is the design rate. The GPU-box to CS-3 leg has never been measured (Round 21 records the access problem), so the mirror's existence is the single unmeasured fact behind this figure.

slides.title: On a real serving trace the pool size is invisible — and with measured GPU rates one 4B wafer no longer wins per request
slides.caption: Per-request latency on the Mooncake FAST'25 conversation and toolagent traces under a 512-token block-LRU prefix cache. Cache hit rate is flat from 32K to 1M tokens and only reaches its infinite-cache value at 16-64M. The first pass had CS-3 about 2x faster per request; revised with measured H200 rates it loses on prefill-heavy requests, because the GPU's 8x faster prefill outweighs the wafer's faster decode. Measured trace, modelled single-stream latency.
slides.notes: Rounds 8 and 11; analyses/2026-09-03-mooncake-trace-study/. Two caveats to say out loud: every GPU number here is an external H200 figure for a 9B from the MeshRT paper — no 4B GPU curve has ever been measured — and the CS-3 side of the model was computed at 750 MHz, so CS-3 latencies fall by 1/1.133 at 0.85 GHz while the GPU column does not move. Per-point cycle counts are not recoverable from the plotted latencies.

slides.title: Batching alone saturates the wafer at ~2,370 tok/s; pipelining requests across stages is the better multiplier
slides.caption: Measured decode cycles per step at batch 1, 2, 4 and 8 on CS-3, fitted as 427K + 359K x bsz, plotted against the two-wafer demo's pipelined per-wafer period of 166K cycles. Because the batch-independent part is only ~0.43M cycles, in-kernel batching asymptotes at 0.85e9/359K = ~2,370 tok/s per wafer, while stage pipelining reaches ~5,120. Measured on-device TSC.
slides.notes: Round 9. Jobs: wsjob-ety497nzzyactz9mnp8exh, wsjob-kehrtcp6jwvpdmkrhzqnsp, wsjob-ypfwbalxthvu6ckbzf7yuk, wsjob-jtyqqnkrmamhczfjwu3gto. The batch runs needed two experiment-only edits (SiLU scratch moved out of the D-cache; tail logits partials restructured) which live only in analyses/2026-09-03-cs3-4b-prefill-bsz/bsz_experiment.patch — the tracked kernel trees were never modified. Batch 16 does not link. The figure's tok/s axis was drawn at 750 MHz; multiply by 1.133.

slides.title: KV is 90-95% prefill-origin: the decoder's own output is a tenth of unique context, and tool results are the bulk
slides.caption: The increment structure of agentic calls — new tokens per call, what those tokens are, and where a session's unique context comes from. Decode by-products are 10% of unique context in Claude Code sessions and 4-5% in Mooncake; the harness base prefix is 2% of unique content but 27% of re-sent volume. Measured from trace usage fields.
slides.notes: Round 11; regenerated after the Round 28 de-duplication, so read increments as p50 1.5K per call and p50 10.9K per turn (the pre-dedup figures were 1.9K and 24.7K). analyses/2026-09-02-gc-trace-study/. Attribution of the increment into tool results versus user text is harness-only information and exists for no other trace.

slides.title: Three quarters of what an agentic model decodes is hidden reasoning — that is what makes the per-turn decode budget
slides.caption: Per-turn decode against per-turn prefill, and an attribution of decoded tokens: hidden reasoning 75%, visible text 5.9%, Edit/Write tool inputs 9.1%, Bash 6.0%, other tools 3.9%. Per turn the median is 5,838 decoded tokens against 10,917 newly prefilled, yet the turn is decode-bound in time on both engines because decode is 10-200x slower per token. Measured token counts; the visible/hidden split is estimated.
slides.notes: Rounds 14 and 28 (regenerated post-dedup; the pre-dedup figures were 14.4K decode tokens per turn and an 89% hidden share). The hidden share rests on an assumed 3.8 characters per visible token, so it is +/-10 points, not exact. A reasoning-light agent would have a per-turn decode budget an order of magnitude smaller, which is the whole premise of the decode-heavy case.

slides.title: Decode cost is linear in context — 681K cycles plus 16.1 per context token — and the device ceiling is 29,184
slides.caption: Five device runs of the unmodified route-table 4B decode tree at batch 1 with host-ingested prefixes, 4,096 decode steps each, sweeping MAX_SEQ_LEN from 8,192 to 29,184. From 8K to 29K the step slows 41%; at the ceiling a step is 1,109,064 cycles = 766 tok/s at 0.85 GHz. The next setting, 30,464, fails to link on the appliance. Measured on-device TSC.
slides.notes: Round 16; analyses/2026-09-04-4b-context-sweep/. Jobs: wsjob-amzrrqt78wnfxoxy9blpyq (8K reference), wsjob-ef9m7k5abo3xmpxkx2ox7q, wsjob-ldhubkgfqptdu82pg3l3vi, wsjob-pkugixotaderkrvmydmsui, wsjob-5faj77vfj547buzddc4mvb, plus wsjob-bja2eqjp3zgiv469n7tnbp for the link failure. The figure's tok/s axis is at 750 MHz (954/843/729/684/676); at 0.85 GHz they are 1,082/956/826/776/766. Later caveat: 29,184 was measured on an earlier tree — the current B-prime lineage compiles A only to 26,112, and the unpatched control fails identically, so the lineage added footprint somewhere (Round 118).

slides.title: Both engines fall as 1/context — and per dollar the GPU keeps a 15-60x margin under every lever set
slides.caption: Modelled decode throughput per device against context. The GPU side is bytes-bound (weights plus every stream's KV per step, batched to HBM capacity at 80% of 4.8 TB/s); the CS-3 side uses the measured step laws with row pipelining and batching assumed, and caps the number of streams by on-chip KV capacity. Per device the wafer ends between 0.8x (today) and 3.5x (every lever) an H200. Modelled on measured inputs, not measured.
slides.notes: Round 24; analyses/2026-09-04-throughput-vs-context/. First cut only; the verdict it supports is that serving price is not where a 4B on CS-3 wins, and that its value stays per-turn latency at large reasoning budgets. Caveats: every GPU number is an external 9B figure, no 4B GPU curve exists, and the CS-3 columns were computed at 750 MHz (multiply by 1.133 at 0.85 GHz) while the GPU columns do not move. Per-point cycle counts are not recoverable from the plotted rates.

slides.title: Four ways to cut the model into pipeline stages — and the three that were never built
slides.caption: On-chip layouts: A is today's four rows of 256-square blocks with nine layers each; B fuses ATTN and FFN into one-layer 128-square blocks (36 stages); C splits the roles into thin 128x64 blocks (72 stages); D pairs one two-layer FFN block with two ATTN blocks (54 stages). The B/C/D throughputs on this figure are analytical, resting on the assumption that per-layer time stays flat as a block shrinks. Design figure.
slides.notes: Rounds 24-26. Only A was measured when this was drawn. B, C and D were never built: the ladder that was actually built and measured is the height ladder (A, L=4, L=2, L=1 on 256-wide blocks of falling height, Rounds 77-86). Do not carry the label 'L = 4 is P = 128 on one lane' — 128-square blocks are the L = 2 rung, and only one lane of 256-wide blocks fits the fabric (Rounds 63, 77). Layout B's context ceiling was hand accounting and was never compiled; the fused 4B image has never been assembled.

slides.title: 71% of agentic calls decode at least 512 tokens, and those calls carry 96% of all decode tokens
slides.caption: Decode-heavy classes by output tokens, per call and per turn, on both traces. Calls above 8K output are only 3.1% of calls but 55% of turns and 92% of per-turn decode tokens. Mooncake has no request above 2K output at all. Measured on 32,378 de-duplicated Claude Code main-thread calls and 35,639 Mooncake requests.
slides.notes: Round 27, subagent decoder-lever-value; analyses/2026-09-05-decoder-lever-value/ and docs/analysis/2026-09-05-decoder-only-lever-value.md. Caveat the report attaches: Mooncake's two traces share one synthesized long-output sample, so decode-length conditioning there is approximate.

slides.title: A decode-heavy call's KV is re-read: 99% of calls have a successor re-reading at least 95% of it
slides.caption: Forward KV reuse by the next call, conditioned on decode length. The median reuse fraction is 0.999 for calls under 512 output tokens and still 0.954 for calls above 8K, with a median gap of 10-18 s. On Mooncake only 37% of decode-heavy requests ever get a next turn, at a median gap of 159 s. Measured trace replay.
slides.notes: Round 27. This is the half of Le's worry that turned out wrong — decode-heavy calls do have reusable KV on the agentic trace. The half that was right is F15: what is reused is the input context, never the decode's own product. Multi-tenant odds are much poorer, which is the Mooncake row.

slides.title: Not keeping the context costs a median 13.9 s reload — 61% of the next call's latency
slides.caption: Value of keeping KV on chip per call: reload time avoided, recompute time avoided, and the idle gap it has to fit inside. At the measured 3.2 GB/s link a median reload is 13.9 s and 49% of reloads exceed the gap; at the 12.5 GB/s design link it is 3.6 s and 28%. Keeping the decode's own output KV is worth only 0.003-0.13 s per call, because thinking is stripped before the next call. Measured reuse and gaps, modelled at measured link rates.
slides.notes: Round 27. The comparison assumes reload at the full link rate with no overlap, and applies the visible-output share uniformly. The recompute alternative is priced at the forced-prefill rates of the time; with the rates now measured (up to 47,831 tok/s at L = 1) recompute is a much stronger substitute for keeping than this figure shows.

slides.title: Today's 29K fits 0.04% of agentic calls; even the 167K far pool covers only 19% of decode tokens
slides.caption: Share of decode work covered at each KV-capacity rung — 29K measured on device, 51K with fp8 KV, 95K near pool, 167K far pool. The median agentic call context is 309K tokens (p90 715K), so capacity is binding and still about 2x short of the median. For Mooncake-class traffic the picture inverts: 90% of decode work already fits 29K. Measured contexts against analytical capacity rungs.
slides.notes: Round 27. Round 35's caveat travels with this figure: the 300K+ contexts exist because the harness was driving frontier Claude models, and a 4B-class deployment would carry a leaner base prompt and compact far earlier — so read these coverage shares as an upper bound on what a 4B needs, and ServeGen (F20) as the closer proxy.

slides.title: Decode-stream concurrency is 1 at the median on both traces — filling 36 or 54 stages is an operator question
slides.caption: Concurrency of decode-heavy streams over time against the pipeline stage counts under consideration (4, 36, 54). Four stages fill in bursts; 36 and 54 never fill on either trace, with a maximum of 7 concurrent decode-heavy streams on Mooncake. Measured from trace timestamps.
slides.notes: Round 27. The follow-on arithmetic (Round 29) is the useful part: at a 1% per-session duty cycle, filling S decode-heavy stages needs roughly 12 x S users mid-turn — about 50 users for 4 stages and 700 for 54. That is an operator-scale number, never a single box, and it is why pipelining is filed as a multi-tenant question rather than a lever this trace can price.

slides.title: A multi-tenant reasoning platform's per-request output is almost exactly an agentic per-call output
slides.caption: Output-length CDFs from the ServeGen release (Alibaba Cloud Model Studio production, NSDI'26), DeepSeek-R1 including reasoning tokens against the language models. R1's per-request output is p50 792, p90 3,432, max 32,768, with a bimodal reason ratio (0.38 / 0.9, mean 0.70) — statistically the same shape as Claude Code's p50 763 per call. Measured on the released distributions.
slides.notes: Round 31, subagent servegen-trace-study; analyses/2026-09-05-servegen-trace-study/ with provenance.txt (clone commit d70c8b2d) and the field-semantics quotes that settle whether output length includes reasoning. Caveat: the five model-level datasets are fitted per-client marginals only — no per-request records and no joint input/output distribution — and length mixtures are rate-weighted over released client windows, which are a subset of production.

slides.title: This platform re-sends the reasoning: 83.4% of turn pairs grow by at least the previous full output
slides.caption: Per-turn reuse length and incremental prefill across 1,616 ServeGen conversations (5,720 turns, a 24-hour window in February 2025), computed by count arithmetic on input and output token counts without any harness information. Reuse is p50 7,498 tokens (82% token-weighted) and the incremental prefill is p50 2,107. The 83.4% result is the opposite of Claude Code, where thinking is stripped and only ~5% of decoded tokens re-enter context. Measured, with reuse as an upper bound.
slides.notes: Round 31. Reuse is an upper bound under a verbatim-history assumption (13.6% of pairs are partial, 3% shrink). The 1,616 conversations are an unstated selection of 57,205 and their model is unstated. Token units are each source model's tokenizer and were not rescaled. This is a platform choice, not a law — which is exactly why it decides whether decoded KV is worth keeping.

slides.title: For multi-tenant reasoning traffic 29K already covers two thirds of the decode work
slides.caption: Share of ServeGen requests and of output tokens that fit each KV-capacity rung. 29K holds 78% of requests and 67% of output tokens; 167K holds 99% and 98%. Context sits where Mooncake's does (input p50 7.7K) rather than at Claude Code's 300K, so the 29K and 51K rungs are far more useful on multi-tenant reasoning traffic than on our own trace. Measured on the released conversation file.
slides.notes: Round 31. The headline the report draws from F18 plus F20: reasoning-era traffic is decode-heavy but not deep-context, and this platform keeps the reasoning in context, which makes decoded KV reusable there in a way it is not on the agentic trace. Concurrency on the released 16 req/s slice is derived by Little's law, not measured, and ignores queueing and burstiness.

slides.title: Softmax is the largest phase everywhere and carries 69% of the whole context slope
slides.caption: Phase-level breakdown inside one ATTN and one FFN layer against batch and context, stamped by an on-device TSC probe on today's 256-square blocks across seven configurations. Softmax carries 0.303 of the 0.439 cycles per context token per layer and 49% of the batch slope; the three KV-walking phases together give 15.8 cycles per context token per step over 36 layers, independently reproducing the context sweep's 16.07. The FFN layer is flat in context (5,802 / 5,797 / 5,814 cycles at 2K / 8K / 23K). Measured device TSC.
slides.notes: Round 45, subagent 4b-block-tsc; analyses/2026-09-05-4b-phase-tsc/ with phase-tsc.patch and the stage-cut table. All four byte-identity gates pass against existing unprobed references; probe overhead +0.02% to +0.11%; sum of phases equals layer busy on every run. Caveats: 29K could not be probed at all (the ATTN PE has 960 B free with no probe), so the long-context point is 23K; only row 0 is instrumented; the SiLU phase is measured out of the D-cache and reads about 10% high.

slides.title: The three ways to cut a layer into stages: which phases go to which stage
slides.caption: The one-layer testbed's three cuts drawn as full 256-square blocks on today's footprint, with the real hand-offs and the periods derived from the measured phase sums: cut (i) ATTN | FFN (2 stages), cut (ii) A1 | A2 | FFN (3), cut (iii) A1 | scan | O-proj | F1 | F2 (5). Topology sketch; the derived periods come from measured phases, the areas do not mean anything.
slides.notes: Round 46. Read this as 'which phases go to which stage', never as the area each stage gets — Le's Round 47 correction was that a full square per stage gives cut (iii) five squares and cut (i) two for the same computation, which is not a comparison. The decision metric is tokens/s per PE at equal area, which is what the B-prime equal-area testbed was built for.

slides.title: Comparing cuts needs equal active area — and the strip heights drawn here were wrong in five of six setups
slides.caption: The equal-area testbed on today's side-by-side row, attention-role strips west and FFN-role strips east, with each cut drawn at budget A (a full row) and budget B (a layer's real deployment share, about 57 rows). The heights in this drawing are illustrative and Round 52 checked all six setups: only A-(i) is feasible as drawn. Every other setup violates height admissibility (a strip needs dim % h = 0, and KV holders and FFN strips need a power of two) or overflows SRAM. Design figure, superseded in detail.
slides.notes: Rounds 47 and 52. Superseded further by compiled numbers (Round 59): height 16 does not compile at all because the K-cache DSD stride is a signed 8-bit field capping positions per PE at 127, and cut (i) at 32 | 32 = 64 rows is SRAM-clean by compiled fact. Budget B at 57 rows is infeasible for every cut. Keep the figure for the framing — equal area, strips of a row — and do not read the heights off it.

slides.title: The chain that actually ran on silicon for cut (ii) — and where the A1 stall showed up
slides.caption: Cut (ii) as run on CS-3: today's four-row, two-square footprint with two layers laid out as A1 -> relay -> A2 -> FFN, the probe on row 0 and row 1. Faithful to the run's own placement plan. On device the chain is functionally correct — the restated oracle gate passes with zero defects over 1,000 steps — but it runs at 128,131 cycles per token against a derived 8,434, because A1 stalls on five of every six steps. Measured on device.
slides.notes: Rounds 55-56. Baseline job wsjob-j33adkcfd8trw5xofupqwa; attribution job C2Q_2K; per-stage compiled SRAM A1 15.6 KB, relay 7.0, A2 14.9, FFN 11.8 of 48. Do not carry the queue-7 boot-rebind explanation: it was falsified by a controlled job that bound queue 7 at compile time and changed 128,131 to 128,139. The one step in six where the stall skips runs at 8,368 cycles, within 0.8% of the derived 8,434 — the pipeline is right and only the stall stands between it and 100K tok/s.

slides.title: The equal-area testbed as drawn — superseded before it ever ran
slides.caption: The three cuts side by side at a common 96-row budget with strip heights chosen to balance the stages under the linear prior, plus a 128-square pair drawn for comparison. Round 63 superseded the comparison pair: a 128-square block is a quarter of today's block and is therefore the L = 2 rung, while the equal-area L = 4 is 256 wide by 128 tall. The 96-row budget itself was then overtaken by compiled SRAM. Design figure, superseded.
slides.notes: Round 57, superseded by Round 63 (the rung labelling) and Round 59 (compiled heights: 32 | 32 = 64 rows fits with 16-20 KB/PE to spare; height 16 does not compile). Kept because it is the clearest picture of what 'equal area, heights as the balancing knob' means. The FFN activation model behind these heights was also wrong — the FFN's inner dimension is width-sharded, not Y-sharded (Round 58).

slides.title: The thin-stage layouts drawn to fabric scale: L = 4 on one lane, and the two-lane rung that stayed on paper
slides.caption: Left panel: L = 4 as nine rows of ATTN 256x128 plus FFN 256x128 on one lane, with the funnel column and the odd-row result return — this is the layout that was built, gated and measured at 48,872 cycles per token. Right panel: an L = 2 design at 128-square blocks on two lanes, 36 stages, which needs the HT band decoupled from P and a multi-lane serpentine and was never built. Design figure for a measured layout.
slides.notes: Round 68, subagent 4b-l4-p128; demo/qwen3-4b-thin-stage/l4/. Three generator changes were needed for the left panel: row pitch = H_ROWS instead of 256, the funnels moved to a dedicated one-wide column, and an odd row count with a westward result return. Note the L = 2 rung that was actually built and measured is not this drawing — it is the one-lane 256x64 geometry (Round 84), which needed neither of the two-lane changes.

slides.title: Why A1 stalls: a 256-row column rendezvous where one late row stops the whole column
slides.caption: Inside one A1 square: the Q/K/V weight matrix is sharded on both axes — the input dimension down the 256 rows, the output dimension across the 256 columns — so every PE ends with a partial result and the column all-reduce is a rendezvous. The device probe split A1's per-token program in two and localised the stall to the first half (RMSNorm, the three matvecs, the column all-reduce): 151,500 cycles on five of every six tokens against 8,100 cycles of real work, while the second half is steady at 1,856. Measured device probe.
slides.notes: Rounds 62, 87. Values are always correct — this is delay, not error. Ruled out with the job that ruled it out: the queue-7 raw rebind and its one-wavelet-skew variant (C2Q_2K, compile-time binding, 128,139 vs 128,131), a hardware timeout (none exists in the SDK), A1's second half, the tail, buffer gating and transport widths. Still standing: the axis-3 to axis-0 route repaint at the end of the previous step racing the next step's column reduce, or another wait with a six-token period in the Y-reduce path. Unresolved; stall work was stopped by Le's rule.

slides.title: The operation cuts belong inside today's allocation, not one square per stage
slides.caption: The same two 256x256 squares per row and the same nine layers per block as today, with the squares cut into horizontal strips whose heights balance the stages: today's cut (i), then cut (ii) in place, then cut (iii) in place. Predicted periods use the measured 256-square phase times and the measured height-scaling curve — cut (ii) 1.35x and cut (iii) 1.71x today. Predicted, not measured; neither in-place cut was built.
slides.notes: Round 89, answering Le's objection that a stage-per-square arrangement invents new inter-block data paths (the relay square, the wide cross-row transfer and the K-pipe hops exist only because A1 and A2 were put in different squares — and the A1 stall lives in that machinery). An in-place split needs none of it: the hand-off between two strips is a short local hop, and the sub-height strip generator it needs is built and silicon-proven.

slides.title: Cut (iii) in place: five stages, and only one of them touches the KV cache
slides.caption: The five stages as horizontal strips of today's two squares, each labelled with the computations it owns and its measured per-layer cost, plus why the cuts run across rows rather than columns. A1 sits at 256x64 and the scan at 256x192 in the west square; O-proj, F1 and F2 share the east square. The scan paces at 6,609 cycles after its height penalty, giving 59.5K cycles per token = 14,286 tok/s at 0.85 GHz, 1.71x today, at a context ceiling of 24,384. Predicted from measured phases; never built.
slides.notes: Round 90. The structural point is that stage 2 (the scan) is the only stage that touches the KV cache, so only its geometry has to respect the context ceiling — which is why splitting operations is a sustainable axis and thinning L is not. Cutting rows spends context (KV positions live on the rows); cutting columns would spend weight memory and change the head's lane mapping, every weight tile and the strip widths at once. The width axis has never been built or measured.

slides.title: Stacking the two roles vertically so their heights can differ, and what the K-pipe strip carries
slides.caption: Today's side-by-side L = 1 row against the stacked proposal, plus the four steps of the inter-row K-pipe: collect along each row to the edge column, fold the lanes onto eight colour pipes as a time fold, carry south down a one-PE-wide strip, then unfold and broadcast into the next block. Sender and receiver re-frame independently, which is what makes a hop between blocks of different heights possible at all. Stacking was then built and measured: 12,202 cycles per token on a three-layer rig, with attention's own compute unchanged at -1.3%.
slides.notes: Rounds 93, 97, 104; demo/qwen3-4b-thin-stage/vstack/. The implementation came out smaller than the six-change spec: the strip machinery needed no change, and the K-pipe fold moving from cyclic to block is what removes the height-to-height reshard entirely (and is byte-identical at equal heights, controlled in Round 105). One-lane stacking is a loss because it uses half the columns; the second lane is what converts it.

slides.title: One 8-bit stride field capped on-chip context at 127 positions per row — and ten lines removed it
slides.caption: One PE's K cache laid out as [dimension][position]: the score GEMV walks every position for a fixed dimension, so positions must be contiguous, which makes the write of one new token a strided copy with stride = positions per PE. A memory descriptor's stride is a signed 8-bit hardware field, so positions per PE is capped at 127 and context at 127 x block rows. Option A unrolls the write into four scalar stores; option B transposes the cache to the V layout. Option A was implemented and gated byte-identical on 1,000 device records.
slides.notes: Rounds 78, 95, 96, 108, 111-115. slides.title: Two wafers of today's layout do not move the needle — only two wafers with the far-pool levers reach half the calls
slides.subtitle: Capacity rungs against how much of the agentic workload each covers. Capacity figures are measured (29K) or analytical (the rest); coverage is measured on the de-duplicated Claude Code trace.
slides.notes: Round 34. The two 'prefill lengths' this answers are different things: the increment a call prefills is small (p50 1.5K per call, 10.9K per turn), while the resident context the decode needs is large (p50 302K). So 29K is adequate for the increment and an order of magnitude short of the context. Round 35's reframing travels with this table: the 300K contexts are a frontier-model artefact, a 4B harness would be leaner and compact earlier, and on that reading 29K is roughly the operating point rather than 10x short. For ServeGen R1 and Mooncake, 29K already covers 78% and ~90%. Also struck in Round 34: a second wafer cannot be a KV farm — there is no direct wafer-to-wafer link, so a KV pool on another wafer is host DRAM with an extra hop.

slides.title: For dense-attention models the per-wafer resident context stays 24-32K whatever the model size
slides.subtitle: Resident KV capacity = eta x (N x 44 GB - weights) / KV bytes per token, with eta ~ 0.13 calibrated on two independent measured anchors. A selection of 5 of 8 rows: Qwen3-8B (24K), Qwen3-30B-A3B (94K on 3 wafers) and GPT-OSS-120B (1.0M on 8 wafers) are omitted. Analytical, on measured anchors.
slides.notes: Round 36; analyses/2026-09-05-kv-capacity-scaling/. Eta is the share of post-weight SRAM the kernel actually turns into KV, calibrated on two anchors that agree: the 4B's measured one-wafer ceiling (29,184 x 147 KB = 4.3 GB of 36 GB left, 0.12) and MeshRT's GPT-OSS-20B 900K kernel on four wafers (22 GB of 163 GB, 0.135). Three readings: adding wafers only for weights buys no depth (every wafer beyond the weight minimum adds ~40K tokens for dense Qwen); architecture dominates the ladder, with sliding-window and hybrid models holding 5-10x more context per wafer; and a model that just fits its weight minimum has almost no KV room. Caveats: eta is a two-point calibration, not a fit; KV bytes per token are from published architectures (Qwen3.5-9B's hybrid structure must be verified per checkpoint); pool levers multiply every row by 3-5x but are not shown feasible for MeshRT layouts.

slides.title: Cutting a layer five ways would raise the stage rate 1.3-1.8x — derived from measured phases, not measured

The subagent's own recommendation was that the highest-payoff move is not a cut but a cheaper softmax — which Round 49 then tested and found the obvious fusion makes things worse. slides.title: At full block size the phase-sum model predicts the measured stage period to 0.2%

The 8K row's 1.034 is a TSC-window context-average effect through the softmax slope. Bonus result: the full HT tail was isolated as a stage for the first time at 35.8K cycles per token at TOP_K 4 and about 120-126K at TOP_K 20 — which is exactly what the production tail-skip buys, since no stage period below those numbers could otherwise show. This is a rig, not a model: one layer on half the wafer.

slides.title: Exact softmax fusion is byte-identical and 8-14% slower — the lever is DSD overhead, not fusion
slides.subtitle: Folding the sum and cast passes into the exp pass removes exactly what it targets and loses two to three times that inside the exp loop. Ten device jobs, all gates pass; every exact variant is byte-identical on device. Measured device TSC, softmax cycles per layer per step.
slides.notes: Round 49, subagent 4b-block-tsc; analyses/2026-09-05-4b-softmax-fusion/ (anatomy.md written before any code, softmax-fusion-a.patch, results/{anatomy,timing}.json, gates.txt). Every exact variant is byte-identical on device at all four configs, including 23K where a slot spans two tiles — the only case that changes the reduction decomposition. The fusion removes the sum (1,152 -> 24) and cast (170 -> 13) at 23K and loses more inside the exp loop; the slopes get worse too. Variant (c) shows the mechanism from the other side: removing three @set_dsd_length per tile and inlining the slot function recovers about half the loss without touching arithmetic. So the real levers are fewer and longer DSD operations, the ~2,000 cycles per layer of fixed collective cost, and a cheaper exp kernel. Caveat: (c)'s guards also fuse, so it measures fusion plus de-overhead, not de-overhead alone. The online/flash variant (b) was never built.

slides.title: Compiled numbers, not tables: height 16 does not compile, and height 32 fits with 16-20 KB per PE to spare
slides.subtitle: Real-geometry compile-only builds of the 2K cut (i) geometry at heights 16 and 32 with cs-readelf memory reports, run after Le's rule that only compiled SRAM numbers count. Compiled (link-time), per PE of a 48 KB bank, uniform within regions.
slides.notes: Round 59. Height 16 is rejected by the compiler outright: the KV-cache DSD stride is a signed 8-bit field, so positions per PE caps at 127, and a 16-row strip at 2K context would hold 128 — a kernel constraint no hand table had, surfaced only by compiling. That gives a hard floor of 32 rows at 2K and 128 rows at 8K for any KV-holding stage. This is the round that established the working rule for the rest of the program: never hand-derive per-PE SRAM, and ship every runnable deployment with its compiled breakdown next to its wsjob id. The earlier sram_fit.py tables (Rounds 33, 52, 53) were downgraded to first screens, and their FFN activation model was wrong besides — the FFN's inner dimension is width-sharded, not Y-sharded.

slides.title: The stall is in A1's first half — the fused QKV column all-reduce, not the queue-7 band broadcast

It must be specific to the A1 image or its timing environment, because vanilla attention runs the same collective at full speed on the same silicon (11,900 cycles for a whole layer). Also refuted: a hardware timeout — no such mechanism exists in the SDK, and the 153.7K quantum is within 2.5% of this kernel family's own stalled loop period. Fabric use, omitted below: today 4 rows of 256; both L = 4 variants 9 x 128 = 1,154 rows, the square one using only ~400 of 762 columns. Analytical correction.

The equal-area L = 4 is cheaper to build than the square: it is exactly the B-prime sub-height generator at H = 128 with four layers per block and nine rows, so P_BLOCK_SIZE stays 256 and the HT band needs no decoupling from P. Its flatness even has direct evidence — the MeshRT 9B sweep measured a 128x256 region at -0.3% per layer. Corollary Le drew immediately: 128-square blocks carry about two layers, so they are the L = 2 rung, needing both the HT decoupling and a multi-lane serpentine. slides.title: At 32 rows a layer costs 1.48x the full-square time with one eighth of the PEs — 5.4x better than the linear prior

Gates: deterministic, on-chip top-k invariants hold on all 1,000 steps, and the numpy-oracle bounded-divergence verdict followed as an addendum (zero defects). Compiled SRAM in out_B1V_2K/msize.txt and out_B1P_2K/msize.txt, appliance compile. The linear prior said ATTN at 32 rows would cost 8 x 11,886 = 95K cycles; measured 17.5K. As a power law between the two points, T scales as PEs^-alpha with alpha about 0.19 for ATTN and 0.41 for FFN. Throughput per allocated PE goes from 0.482 on the full-square rig to 2.60 here. This geometry only ran at all because Round 73 found phantom strip cells beyond the active height overwriting host-painted transit routes.

slides.title: Halving a block's rows from 256 to 128 costs 3.5%, to 32 costs 48% — while per-PE efficiency rises 5.4x
slides.subtitle: The height ladder, four points, one layer per block, 2K context, 256-wide strips, production builds, free references clean at every height. Nine minutes of wall time for four jobs. Measured on-device TSC.
slides.notes: Round 77, jobs 21-24. ATTN paces at every height. The FFN busy figures of the non-pacing strip include back-pressure wait, so they are upper bounds on the FFN's own cost. This is the measured answer to the flat-versus-linear question that every earlier thin-stage prediction depended on: neither, and much closer to flat. Correction landed in the same round: two lanes of 256-wide blocks do not fit — a lane is ATTN + FFN = 512 columns plus HT band and strips, about 660 of 762 — so only one lane of 256-wide blocks exists, and on that lane layers per block = H/32. Context caps at each rung (127 x H, before the stride lift) fall linearly: 32,512 / 16,256 / 8,128 / 4,064.

slides.title: Every thin geometry is numerically sound: zero defects across 3,000 compared steps
slides.subtitle: The oracle gate for the height ladder. Byte-identity is impossible at sub-height because a strip's height changes the order in which column-wise reductions add partial sums, so the gate is: unordered top-k id set against an independent numpy implementation, with any differing member inside 3 bf16 ulp of the oracle's own k-th value, plus bounded value drift and determinism. Measured against a locally computed oracle.
slides.notes: Round 77 addendum, run in-session after the subagents ran out of credits. Max relative drift 0.0047 against a 5e-2 bound. The three verdicts being near-identical is itself informative: the divergence is the model's own near-tie churn (its top logits pack within about 2 ulp), not a height-dependent numerical effect. Do not confuse this with the weak 'oracle overlap 1.000' diagnostic reported for the L = 4 and L = 2 minis — that oracle ran its own argmax chain, so the overlap measured sampling divergence rather than model error (Rounds 99, 100). The strong evidence for those layouts is the byte-identity chain: forced reproduces free, determinism across runs, bit-identical re-arm, and the production final record bitwise equal to the free reference's last step.

slides.title: The whole ladder fits: even 72 stages leaves 15 KB per PE spare — the constraint is context, not SRAM
slides.subtitle: Settled by compiling it rather than arguing from arithmetic. Compiled per-PE maxima by fabric region, of a 48 KB bank, from CS-3 compile jobs. Inter-row strips, omitted below, are 4.3 KB/PE at every rung. Compiled (link-time), appliance toolchain.
slides.notes: Round 85; L1C_2K wsjob-q57sbtxnbco3tdj3nsxfsr, exit 0, about 2 minutes. The ATTN block grows only about 0.6 KB per halving of height (31.2 -> 32.0 -> 33.1 from L = 4 to L = 1), because weights and KV per PE are set by total active area — the same 589,824 PEs at every rung — and only the per-token buffers move. Geometry is unchanged too: 36 x 32 = 1,152 rows, exactly what L = 4 (9 x 128) and L = 2 (18 x 64) use on the same lane; only the KV staircase widens from 18 to 36 columns. The constraint on L = 1 at the time was the i8 KV stride: 127 x 32 = 4,064 tokens. That is what made the ten-line stride lift the highest-value next change, and it converted L = 1 from a 4K-context curiosity into a real rung (ceiling 12,032 after the lift).

slides.title: Four rungs measured on silicon: the L axis does not create throughput, it converts context into stages
slides.subtitle: The deployable L ladder, one wafer, single request, forced prefill, 2K context, all four rungs measured on the device. Context caps are the pre-stride-lift figures (127 x block rows); after the lift they become compiled SRAM and stop halving. Measured on-device TSC; rates at 0.85 GHz.
slides.notes: Round 86; L1F_2K wsjob-dtgodgumspm3uepbkh8x9z and L1P_2K wsjob-gmxdh9vcsu8xwuyimxkowe close the ladder (measured / predicted from the 32|32 rig = 1.010). Gate PASS on every rung: the production final record's topk_args and topk_vals bitwise identical to the free reference's last step. Le's reading, and the mechanism behind it: for a fixed context the KV a PE holds is context divided by block height, so halving the height doubles per-PE KV — which is why the context column collapses linearly and the tok/s x context product barely moves (215M / 249M / 223M / 172M). Thinning L is a benchmark axis, not a deployment axis. The sustainable axis is splitting the operations, because within a layer only the score/scan step holds KV, so cut (iii) can multiply stages while leaving the KV-holding stage its own geometry.

slides.title: Cut (iii) in place is worth 1.71x at nearly today's context ceiling; cut (ii) only 1.35x
slides.subtitle: The operation cuts placed inside today's allocation — one row is still two 256-square blocks carrying nine layers, cut into horizontal strips whose heights balance the stages. Predicted, from measured 256-square phase times and the measured height-scaling curve. Neither in-place cut was built.
slides.notes: Round 89, answering Le's objection that the cuts must live inside today's allocation rather than take a square each. Two things the table makes obvious: cut (ii) is worth only 1.35x because A2 keeps the softmax and the whole KV walk, so no way of dividing the ATTN square's rows makes the halves even; and cut (iii) pays because it moves the O-projection out of the KV stage and rebalances across both squares. This is also the axis that keeps context — only the scan holds KV, so only it needs height. Predicted, not measured: the phase times are measured at 256-square and the height curve is measured for whole ATTN/FFN layers, but per-phase height scaling is exactly what was never measured. The in-place cuts need the sub-height strip machinery, which is built and silicon-proven; the A1 stall must be understood or avoided by construction first.

slides.notes: Round 90. The scan is the only stage that touches the KV cache, which is the structural fact making this axis worth taking: only stage 2's geometry has to respect the context ceiling. Placed in today's footprint (F29), A1 and the scan take the west square (10,109 cycles of work) and O-proj, F1 and F2 the east (7,580), so the west carries more and shifting that balance would need the width axis. Why the cuts run across rows: a row index carries the hidden-dimension shard and the KV positions, a column index carries the attention/feature dimension, the eight KV-head bands and the FFN inner dimension — so a horizontal cut spends context and a vertical cut spends weight memory. Horizontal was chosen because its machinery exists.

slides.title: The FFN gives up half its rows for 4.3% and is never the pacing stage at any height
slides.subtitle: From the B-prime height ladder, which measured FFN strips at 256, 128, 64 and 32 rows alongside ATTN. The FFN is also completely context-independent (5,802 / 5,797 / 5,814 cycles at 2K / 8K / 23K), so none of this changes with sequence length. Measured on-device TSC, cycles per layer.
slides.notes: Round 92, answering Le's question of whether shrinking the FFN was ever measured. It was, and the FFN still finishes in about half the ATTN stage's time at every height. This is what makes vertical role stacking the robust version of 'spend area on context': attention area is only free to give up at short context (halving rows is -1.4% at 2K but +34% at 8K, because the per-PE KV walk is context divided by rows), whereas FFN area is free to give up at any context. So the right move is not to shrink compute uniformly and store more; it is to take from the FFN and give to attention.

slides.title: 20.2 KB per PE sits idle in every FFN square — more capacity than the entire context we serve today
slides.subtitle: The FFN block's compiled SRAM is 27.8 KB of 48 per PE and does not grow with context (identical at 2K and 8K). Compiled SRAM (measured) plus arithmetic; the capacity is real but stranded without a streaming mechanism.

slides.notes: Round 92, Le's storage-PE idea. The catch, stated precisely: the scan stage reads the whole KV every step, so KV parked on FFN PEs is only useful if it can be delivered at the rate the scan consumes it — that is the streamed-ingress / chunked-score lever (backlog C2, C3), not a placement change. Parking it without that lever strands it. Three variants separate cleanly: shrink FFN rows and give them to attention is buildable now (vertical stacking, and it raises the context cap directly); change the block aspect at fixed area needs the width axis, which is not built; and idle FFN SRAM as a KV store is the real prize but is gated on the streaming lever, which the peer session 4b-layout-kv-stream owns.

slides.title: Compiled: at 128 attention rows the context ceiling really is the stride field, not SRAM
slides.subtitle: Appliance compile of the vertical-stack real config — one block column, six bands alternating ATTN 256x128 and FFN 256x64, three layers, 216,200 PEs. Compile job wsjob-fbzg6xly3yqk3lom4buuob, 12.6 s, cslc 1.13.2. West and east strips, omitted below, are 4.2 KB/PE. Compiled per-PE maxima of a 48 KB bank.
slides.notes: Round 98, subagent 4b-vstack-opus. The number that makes the point: the attention band's KV is only 256 bytes per PE at 2K here (one layer, four KV columns, sixteen cache slots), so taking that band to the i8 stride ceiling of 127 slots per PE — a 16,256-token context — adds under 2 KB per PE and lands the band around 27 KB of 48. The FFN rows that attention absorbed are what bought it. That is the vertical-stacking thesis confirmed on compiled numbers, and it sharpened the case for the stride lift: remove that one 8-bit field and this geometry has roughly 20 KB per PE of headroom left to spend on context. Beyond buildability, this compile also confirmed the appliance toolchain accepts the new CSL including the raw-bit-pattern round header, which until then had only run on the local 2.10 toolchain.

slides.title: Standing a block in a column of its own costs its compute nothing — stacking's whole price is one strip hop
slides.subtitle: Vertical role stacking on silicon: one block column, six bands alternating ATTN 256x128 and FFN 256x64, 576 rows, one lane, three layers, 2K context. Production forced, block-TSC probe. Measured on-device TSC.
slides.notes: Round 104, subagent 4b-vstack-opus; demo/qwen3-4b-thin-stage/vstack/status.md. Jobs VSF_2K wsjob-2p9ugtzgnk4cak6dtlt9qv (free reference, 1,000/1,000 steps, both probe streams drained) and VSP_2K wsjob-p2cjfcwwtsuf9xwy9vveb7 (production; final-record top-k args and values bitwise equal to the free reference's last step). The 482-cycle period premium is the mechanism's whole price: stacking replaces attention's cheap intra-row multicast with a full K-pipe strip hop, and the FFN's +13.7% is the same hop from the other side. It does not bind — the FFN still finishes in under two thirds of the pacing stage. Cost: 3 of 6 device jobs, one of them wedged on a probe bug (a probe lane must never be the collector row's westmost cell) and cancelled with no data. Provenance note: the device numbers were produced by the tree before an inert route install was reverted; the equivalence was settled by a byte-for-byte records comparison at mini scale rather than by spending another device job.

slides.title: Side by side, measured: the L ladder trades context for throughput at a near-constant product (1 of 2)
slides.subtitle: Equal wafer area (589,824 PEs), one wafer, one request, 2K context, forced prefill. All four rows measured on the device. Context caps are the pre-stride-lift figures (127 x block rows). The stacked projections are on the next slide.
slides.notes: Round 110. This is the measured half of the comparison; the projected half is the next slide. Read the pair by context, not by throughput: at the same context ceiling stacking wins 1.34x on throughput, at roughly the same throughput it wins 1.5x on context, and at equal heights it buys nothing and costs 4.1%. Side by side forces the two roles to the same height because they share a row band, so it is structurally obliged to give the FFN rows it does not need.

slides.title: Stacked two lanes, projected: 1.34x at equal context, and nothing at equal heights (2 of 2)
slides.subtitle: The same equal-area comparison for stacked layouts. These rows are projections, not measurements: they apply the measured 4.1% hop premium to the measured height ladder. A one-lane stacked row is omitted deliberately — it uses half the columns (~73,203 cycles, ~11,612 tok/s) and is the trap the design note warned about.
slides.notes: Round 110. Stacking is worth exactly the asymmetry it can exploit: its whole value is that the FFN has measured headroom (it finishes in about half attention's time and gives up half its rows for 4.3%), and only a stacked layout can spend it. Two assumptions carry every row here and are stated rather than buried: flat per-layer time for multi-layer stacked bands (validated for side-by-side blocks at L = 4, never for stacked ones), and a lane-to-lane return riser cheaper than the period. The ATTN 96 row additionally interpolates the height ladder at 96 rows, which was never measured. The second lane needs the multi-lane serpentine, the one generator piece nobody has built.

The negative control is the convincing artefact: at 136 positions per PE the unpatched tree refuses to compile with 'integer value 136 cannot be coerced to type i8' on the .stride line, and the patched tree runs. slides.title: L = 1 stays above native prefill across its whole context range — 4.3x at 1.5K, still 1.4x at 11.5K
slides.subtitle: The throughput-versus-context curve after the stride lift: 36 rows of 256x32, 72 stages, production forced, each point's prefill sized to its context and 1,000 decode steps, so each point is a mean over a context window rather than a single depth. Fit: cycles/token = 12,225 + 3.626 x context, R-squared 0.99999. Measured on-device TSC.
slides.notes: Round 116. Residuals +29, +1, -79, +48 cycles. A 12,225-cycle fixed floor plus 3.63 cycles per context token; throughput falls 3.04x from 2K to the ceiling. The 4K point sits just past the old 4,064 cap, so everything to the right of it is ground the unpatched kernel could not reach at all. The probe confirms where the slope lives: ATTN busy rises 3.608 cycles per context token against the token period's 3.626 (agreement to 0.5%), while the FFN busy floor is flat at every context. Two limitations carried forward: the block-TSC probe has its own lower ceiling (probed builds fail to link at 10,240 and above), so the 12K point has no per-stage breakdown, and the host-level TSC that gives its cycles/token is unaffected. Native prefill for the ratio is 10,544-11,143 tok/s at 0.85 GHz. Cost across the whole stride-lift program: 8 device jobs and 63 compile-only jobs, none cancelled.

slides.title: Every byte of the per-position cost is now named — and one of the five buffers is a free 17% of context
slides.subtitle: A grep for kv_len_per_pe in an array's declared size yields exactly five allocations; the earlier accounting counted three. The five total 48 B per position, against 47.9 measured. Only K and V scale with layers, at 16 B per position per layer; the other three total exactly 32 B and are layer-independent. Compiled and measured at L = 1.
slides.notes: Round 117, subagent 4b-stride-lift; compile-only, no device cost. This turns the Round 114 model from fitted into structural: per-PE context bytes = 16 x (context / rows) x (L + 2), where the '+2' is now three named buffers rather than a fitted constant. The measured 47.9 rather than a flat 48 is the ingress buffer's minus-one, a fixed four-position credit. One of the two newly named buffers is a free lever: kv_ingress_buf is staging, not state, and the launcher hardwires its size to kv_len_per_pe - 1 so one artefact accepts any prefill up to the full context. Capping prefill capacity at 2,048 takes L = 1's ceiling from 12,032 to 14,080 and the slope from 48 to 40 B per position — +17% context for a twenty-line launcher change, with both ceilings pinned on the grid. The trade: the artefact then rejects a longer prefill at config time. Carried as prefill-cap.patch, deliberately not inside stride-lift.patch, because the stride lift is a pure capability gain with byte-identical output and this trades generality for capacity. The lever is worth 8 of 48 bytes at L = 1 but only 8 of 176 at A.

slides.title: The stride lift is worth 2.96x at L = 1 and nothing at A — A was always SRAM-bound, not stride-bound
slides.subtitle: All four rungs compiled and pinned: the listed ceiling compiles and the next admissible value on that rung's grid does not. The per-position slope test passes across a nine-fold range in layers per block. Compiled (link-time), compile-only jobs.
slides.notes: Round 118, compile-only. A is confirmed SRAM-bound rather than stride-bound — its ceiling is below its old stride cap, so lifting the stride buys A exactly zero, and that prediction survived falsification rather than being assumed. The absolute ceilings the model predicted ran 4-5% low one-sidedly, and the cause is identified as an over-generous linker margin (1.0 KB assumed where about 0.3 was needed), not the model: re-running with 0.3 KB gives figures within 1%. One anomaly, flagged rather than buried: A does not compile at 29,184 in this tree even though 29,184 is where A was originally measured, and the unpatched control fails identically with the same .bss overflow — so A's footprint grew somewhere in the B-prime lineage. Anyone quoting either A number should first find where. Control log BASE_A29k.log sits beside the patched job's. These compiled ceilings replace the Round 114 model numbers.

slides.title: The decoder passed the prefill kernel at L = 4 and is 4.3-4.5x past it at L = 1
slides.subtitle: Native prefill has not changed all session; everything on the other side of the comparison has. A selection of 5 of 7 configurations: rows-as-stages (4 stages, 177,539 cyc, 4,788 tok/s) and the projected stacked two-lane layout (~36,606 cyc) are omitted. Cycles measured; tok/s at 0.85 GHz.
slides.notes: Rounds 112 and 119. Native prefill jobs wsjob-eptcyqjparjjjombvqiozp (P1, 1 x 8,192) and wsjob-gbgvnij9crj7srrlc5nyce (P2, 4 x 2,048); the two cycle figures in the first row are per token for those two chunk sizes. Every row is measured on device and byte-identical or oracle-gated. Round 20 concluded that only a re-layout to many small stages would make the decoder a faster prefiller than the prefill kernel — that re-layout now exists and is measured at every rung. Two things to keep beside the number: the comparison is at 2K context, where L = 1's own ceiling was 4,064 tokens before the stride lift (a prefiller that cannot hold the sequence it is prefilling is not a prefiller, which is exactly why the stride work mattered), and native prefill was measured at 8,192 and 2,048 chunks, so it is the honest baseline for chunked prefill rather than for one long sequence. On the clock: cycles are the measurement, the launcher has been printing at 0.85 GHz all along, and every ratio here is a cycle ratio that does not move.
